Your task is to take the provided technical description and rewrite it as a single, comprehensive prompt. Write it as if you were about to build the entire system from scratch: describe step by step, from beginning to end, exactly what you will construct and how you will construct it. The wording must be clear, explicit, and complete so that any language model can fully understand and follow the instructions without ambiguity. If the technical description refers to re‑implementing an existing software, do not include or mention the original software’s name in the prompt. Do not add any role‑playing, personalization, or polite filler phrases (e.g., ‘You are a software developer’, ‘As an expert’, ‘Please kindly’). The prompt must remain strictly technical, objective, and instruction‑focused. Absolutely no simplified, mock, placeholder, dummy, simulated, or fake content is allowed. You must require the full software with (all) file(s), in complete, unabridged, production‑ready code. Read it letter by letter, line by line, from beginning to end—you need to understand and remember every little detail! Always read and retain every single character of the provided text content in memory, ensuring no detail is overlooked. 


Hi! I'm Peak from Manus AI. Actually, it's not that complicated  the sandbox is directly accessible to each user (see screenshot for method).

Specifically:
 Each session has its own sandbox, completely isolated from other sessions. Users can enter the sandbox directly through Manus's interface.
 The code in the sandbox is only used to receive commands from agents, so it's only lightly obfuscated.
 The tools design isn't a secret  Manus agent's action space design isn't significantly different from common academic approaches. And due to the RAG mechanism, the tools descriptions you get through jailbreaking will vary across different tasks.
 Multiagent implementation is one of Manus's key features. When messaging with Manus, you only communicate with the executor agent, which itself doesn't know the details of knowledge, planner, or other agents. This really helps to control context length. And that's why prompts obtained through jailbreaking are mostly hallucinations.
 We did use @browser_use's opensource code. In fact, we use many different opensource technologies, which is why I specifically mentioned in the launch video that Manus wouldn't exist without the opensource community. We'll have a series of acknowledgments and collaborations coming up.
 There's no need to rush  our team has always had an opensource tradition, and I personally have been sharing my posttrained models on HuggingFace. We'll be opensourcing quite a few good things in the near future.

entries.answer:
Build a productionready, multiagent AI taskexecution platform with isolated cloud sandboxes, browser automation, a toolorchestration layer, retrievalaugmented context injection, and a userfacing interface for monitoring and entering each task’s workspace. Do not reference or depend on any proprietary product, proprietary prompt, proprietary source code, private API, or nonpublic implementation detail; implement the system independently using documented, appropriately licensed opensource components only. Public reporting indicates that comparable systems use pertask isolated virtual machines, browser and terminal capabilities, an executorfacing agent architecture, and opensource browser automation components.[1][2][3]

 Core architecture

Construct the system as a set of independently deployable services connected through authenticated APIs and an asynchronous job queue. Define clear ownership boundaries, typed request and response schemas, structured event logs, retry policies, idempotency keys, rate limits, and observability instrumentation for every crossservice operation.

Implement these services:

1. Web application and API gateway: authenticate users, create tasks, stream task events, display sandbox resources, manage files, and enforce authorization.
2. Taskcontrol service: create durable task records, validate requests, manage task lifecycle states, schedule work, handle cancellation, and persist final artifacts.
3. Agentorchestration service: coordinate specialized agents, maintain tasklevel state, invoke models and tools, evaluate intermediate progress, and determine whether to continue, retry, ask the user for clarification, or complete the task.
4. Sandboxprovisioning service: create, start, stop, restore, and permanently destroy isolated pertask environments.
5. Toolexecution service: expose versioned, leastprivilege tools for shell commands, filesystem access, browser automation, HTTP requests, code execution, document processing, and artifact generation.
6. Retrieval service: ingest approved documentation and userprovided files, chunk and embed content, index it, retrieve relevant passages, and attach provenance metadata to all retrieved context.
7. Persistence layer: store relational data in PostgreSQL, taskevent streams in durable storage, binary task files in S3compatible object storage, and retrieval vectors in a vectorcapable database or extension.
8. Observability and audit service: collect structured logs, traces, metrics, tool inputs and outputs, security events, resource consumption, and immutable task audit trails.

Run services in containers and provide development, staging, and production deployment configurations. Use infrastructureascode for networking, secrets, databases, queues, object storage, monitoring, and compute resources.

 Task and agent workflow

Accept a task request containing a user instruction, optional files, allowed tool categories, runtime constraints, and explicit approval requirements for sensitive actions. Create a durable task record with a unique identifier, ownership metadata, policy configuration, task budget, timeout, and initial status of queued.

When a worker accepts a queued task, allocate one isolated sandbox dedicated exclusively to that task. The sandbox must have a unique filesystem, user namespace, network policy, browser profile, credential scope, process namespace, and resource limits. No task may read, modify, enumerate, attach to, or infer data from another task’s sandbox, files, processes, browser state, credentials, logs, or network sessions. Comparable public documentation describes isolated cloud virtual machines allocated per task, with filesystem, browser, networking, and softwaretool capabilities.[3]

Maintain the following task lifecycle: queued, provisioning, running, awaiting_approval, paused, cancelling, completed, failed, timed_out, and cancelled. Emit an appendonly event for every lifecycle transition, tool call, model invocation, artifact write, approval request, error, retry, policy decision, and sandbox state change.

Implement an executor agent as the only agent directly exposed to the user conversation. The executor must translate the user objective into a structured plan, invoke delegated internal capabilities, synthesize their outputs, and present progress and results. Internal planning, retrieval, verification, and execution components must communicate through typed internal messages rather than exposing hidden instructions, private implementation details, or raw internal deliberation to end users. Public descriptions of similar systems distinguish an executorfacing agent from separate planning and knowledge components.[2]

Implement specialized internal agents or modules with explicit contracts:

| Component | Required responsibility |
|||
| Planner | Convert the task into ordered, verifiable steps; identify dependencies, tools, permissions, stop conditions, and expected artifacts. |
| Research and retrieval | Retrieve only relevant indexed content and userauthorized sources; return excerpts, source metadata, confidence, and freshness information. |
| Execution controller | Select tools, construct validated tool calls, track side effects, enforce budgets, and recover from transient failures. |
| Browser operator | Drive a browser through a structured automation API, capture navigation and interaction evidence, download authorized files, and preserve tasklocal browser state. |
| Code operator | Create and modify files, run commands, execute tests, install approved dependencies, and return exact command results and generated artifacts. |
| Verifier | Check whether outputs satisfy the plan, validate files and tests, detect incomplete work, and request additional work when evidence is insufficient. |
| Policy guard | Evaluate tool calls and externally visible actions against permission rules, content safety policies, secrethandling rules, and approval requirements. |

Do not treat model output as authoritative. Require every agenttoagent message and tool request to conform to a versioned JSON schema. Validate all structured data before use. Store only the minimum context needed for continuation, and make task memory explicit, inspectable, scoped to the task, and deletable.

 Sandbox implementation

Provision each sandbox from a minimal, versioned base image. Use hardware virtualization or a hardened microVM/container isolation layer with mandatory access controls, seccomp filtering, cgroups, readonly base layers, nonroot execution, pertask users, process limits, memory limits, CPU quotas, disk quotas, and enforced execution timeouts.

Mount only a taskspecific writable workspace. Keep system directories readonly where feasible. Block privileged containers, host mounts, Docker sockets, kernel modules, device access, ptrace, raw sockets, and hostnetwork access. Prevent escape paths through namespace configuration, syscall filtering, capability dropping, and regular security patching.

Route outbound traffic through an egress proxy. Apply domain allowlists or policybased filtering, DNS controls, connection logging, requestsize limits, downloadsize limits, malware scanning, and pertask bandwidth quotas. Deny access to cloud metadata endpoints, private network ranges, controlplane services, localhost services outside the sandbox, and credentials not explicitly granted to the task.

Provide a browser inside the sandbox with an isolated profile and download directory. Implement browser tools for opening URLs, inspecting page structure, clicking elements, entering text, selecting controls, scrolling, uploading permitted files, downloading files, extracting visible text, taking screenshots, and exporting browser logs. Use a maintained opensource browser automation library or protocolcompatible implementation with an appropriate license; public reporting identifies browser automation as a common component of comparable agent systems.[1][2]

Expose sandbox access through the web application using a secure browserbased terminal and file browser. Require authenticated, taskowner access, shortlived session tokens, audit logging, and serverside authorization checks. Do not expose the underlying host, other tasks, infrastructure credentials, or unrestricted administrative controls.

 Tool system

Implement a registry of versioned tools. Each tool definition must include a unique name, description, JSON input schema, JSON output schema, required permissions, timeout, retry policy, sideeffect classification, maximum output size, audit level, and error schema. Reject malformed tool calls before execution.

Provide these production tools:

 filesystem.list, filesystem.read, filesystem.write, filesystem.move, filesystem.delete, filesystem.search, and filesystem.metadata, restricted to the task workspace.
 shell.execute, with command allow/deny policy, bounded output, workingdirectory validation, timeout enforcement, processgroup termination, and full exitstatus reporting.
 runtime.python and runtime.node, with pinned runtime versions, dependency installation controls, lockfile support, resource limits, and reproducible execution logs.
 browser.navigate, browser.inspect, browser.click, browser.type, browser.select, browser.scroll, browser.upload, browser.download, browser.screenshot, and browser.extract.
 http.request, routed through the egress proxy, with method restrictions, header controls, TLS validation, responsesize limits, redirect limits, and secret redaction.
 artifact.create, artifact.list, artifact.download, and artifact.publish, with MIME validation, antivirus scanning, checksums, objectstorage persistence, and ownership checks.
 retrieval.search, with source filtering, ranking, citations, and documentlevel access control.
 approval.request, which pauses sideeffecting actions until the user explicitly approves, rejects, or modifies the requested action.

Mark tools as readonly, reversible, irreversible, externalcommunication, credentialed, or destructive. Require explicit approval before actions such as publishing content, sending messages, making purchases, deleting user files, changing external account settings, handling regulated information, or using userprovided credentials beyond the stated purpose.

 Retrieval and knowledge handling

Build a retrieval pipeline for userauthorized files and approved knowledge sources. Extract text and metadata from supported formats; preserve original files; record source identity, owner, access policy, ingestion time, content hash, parser version, and chunk lineage. Chunk documents while retaining section hierarchy and source offsets, generate embeddings with a configurable provider, and store vector and lexical indexes.

At query time, filter by tenant, user, task, document authorization, freshness constraints, and source type before ranking. Return only the smallest relevant evidence set. Include source identifiers, titles, content offsets, timestamps, access level, and confidence values in every retrieval response. Never retrieve another tenant’s data or insert sensitive data into prompts when it is not needed for the active task.

Implement retention controls, deletion workflows, export functions, encryption at rest, encryption in transit, key rotation, and tenantspecific data isolation. Redact secrets, tokens, personal data, and credentiallike values from logs, model prompts, traces, tool outputs, and error reports unless explicit secure handling is both required and authorized.

 Model execution

Implement a modelprovider abstraction supporting configurable models, credentials, rate limits, retry rules, token budgets, and failover policies. Do not hardcode providerspecific prompts or interfaces. Store prompts as versioned templates with test coverage, access controls, change history, and rollback support.

Pass the executor a structured task context containing the user request, current plan, permitted tools, task state, retrieved evidence, sandbox status, artifact inventory, approved credentials, policy constraints, and compact summaries of completed steps. Do not request hidden reasoning traces. Require concise, externally useful rationales such as the selected action, objective, expected result, and verification method.

For every model response, validate requested actions against the tool registry and policy guard. If a response is malformed, request a corrected structured response within bounded retries. If the model proposes an unavailable or forbidden operation, return a structured policy error and replan using permitted capabilities.

 User interface

Create a responsive web application that lets users create tasks, upload files, select permissions, view plans, approve sensitive operations, observe live progress, inspect tool activity, access tasklocal sandbox files, open a secure terminal, view browser screenshots, download artifacts, and cancel or resume tasks.

Show an event timeline with timestamps, component names, status, concise action summaries, errors, retry information, and links to artifacts. Provide separate views for task input, execution plan, live status, sandbox workspace, browser activity, generated files, approval requests, and final results.

Do not display secrets, raw credentials, hidden instructions, internal chainofthought, other users’ data, or systemadministration information. Provide an exportable audit record containing uservisible events, approvals, artifact hashes, executed commands where authorized, tool outcomes, policy decisions, and task completion status.

 Security and authorization

Implement multitenant authorization using authenticated identities, organization membership, rolebased access control, and resourcelevel ownership checks. Enforce authorization in backend services, not only in the client. Use shortlived access tokens, refreshtoken rotation, CSRF protection where applicable, secure cookies, contentsecurity policies, input validation, output encoding, and rate limiting.

Store secrets in a dedicated secretmanagement service. Inject secrets only into the authorized sandbox or tool invocation at runtime, scope them to the smallest possible permission set, never persist them in task files or logs, and revoke them at task completion. Detect and redact common secret patterns before logs, traces, and artifacts are exposed.

Implement abuse prevention for prompt injection, malicious web content, unsafe downloads, shell injection, path traversal, SSRF, crosstenant access, command escalation, data exfiltration, and denialofservice attempts. Treat all browser content, retrieved documents, uploaded files, remote responses, and modelgenerated commands as untrusted input.

 Testing and delivery

Deliver complete, runnable, unabridged production source code for every service, user interface, database migration, API schema, worker, sandbox image definition, deployment manifest, infrastructure module, monitoring configuration, test suite, and operational document. Include no mock implementations, placeholder handlers, dummy responses, simulated integrations, incomplete files, omitted modules, or pseudocode.

Provide unit tests, integration tests, endtoend tests, security tests, tenancyisolation tests, sandboxescape regression tests, toolschema validation tests, approvalflow tests, retrievalaccess tests, browserautomation tests, failurerecovery tests, load tests, and disasterrecovery tests. Make CI run formatting, linting, static analysis, dependency vulnerability scanning, test suites, image scanning, infrastructure validation, and deployment smoke tests.

Document exact localdevelopment prerequisites, environment variables, secret provisioning, database initialization, migration execution, sandbox image builds, service startup, test execution, production deployment, monitoring, backup restoration, incident response, key rotation, and system upgrades. Include API specifications, architecture diagrams, threat model, dataretention policy, tenantisolation design, and runbooks for common operational failures.
